Five Tips Actors Can Learn From Meisner’s Technique
By admin
20 Aug 2020
0 Comments
You’ve been self-isolating for a while now. You’ve finished watching all of the Netflix shows; you experimented with cooking every possible dish in your fridge; you’ve been exercising and mastering an accent like a pro. That’s all good, but what can we do next? Perhaps you can consider including some new acting tips through Meisner’s techniques at home.
Sandford Meisner was a well-known actor based in New York (you can read more about him here ). He was one of those curious actors along with Stella Adler (we talked about her in our previous post: link here in case you missed it) that adopted Stanislavski’s technique (also known as Method Acting) until he felt the need to develop his own acting form, which is known as the Meisner Technique. It conveys naturalism and focuses on building up tension between acting partners.
Using these techniques will help you become a better actor by allowing yourself to be wholly in the moment with your scene partners. You may have to create a zoom meeting with your scene partner for one of the exercises, but what could be a better reason to meet up with someone again than rehearsing with them!
The Meisner technique has three main components that all work hand-in-hand:
Whilst reading the line, learn to delve into a given circumstance that will generate real emotions. Be in the character’s shoes and think how you would react if that particular situation happened.
By repeating your lines, it can make you rely on their organic instincts.
As you are getting used to the flow of the lines, improv will encourage spontaneity and reduce an actor’s self-consciousness, and these two exercises will let you understand what the technique is about.
1st Exercise:
Actor 1: Your hair is long.
Actor 2: My hair is long.
Actor 1: Your hair is long.
Actor 2: My hair is long.
A: (Noticing B scratched their arm) You scratched your arm.
B: I scratched my arm.
This activity removes the over-thinking part of acting, and even after a short period of time, one realises the ‘text’ becomes essentially irrelevant, and it is the subtext and relationship that really matter. It lets you be more observant of your acting partner and enables you to be more perceptive of the body language of each other.
2nd Exercise:
When reading the lines, recall a memory where you were in that circumstance and apply that emotion to the scene.
If it’s not a circumstance you had any experience of, you can draw external sources of research, e.g. asking friends or family, watching interviews, reading books, and people-watching, to gather a library of additional material to provide inspiration.
In conclusion, as you try out these exercises, you will feel differently when acting because you’ll be facing the “given circumstances” of the character with different points of view. These techniques can help you to be more observant and to analyse the tension between you and your partner to be inspired and provoke your acting decisions. Ultimately, it will make you listen and react with clarity, which is really what acting is all about.
Let us know if these techniques can help you and get in touch if you wish to share thoughts and ideas!
